searches.description:
Identify T. brucei genes based on comparisons of RNAi target sequencing coverage at different life cycle stages. Genes returned by this search have coverage (RPKM) values in Comparison Sample(s) that is less than that of the Uninduced Control.

In this experiment an RNAi plasmid library, containing randomly sheared genomic fragments was used to create an inducible library in bloodstream form T. brucei. After transfection, the library was grown under non-inducing and inducing conditions and genomic DNA was isolated from surviving populations. Adapter-ligated sequencing libraries were prepared from each genomic DNA sample and used to amplify DNA fragments containing RNAi cassette-insert junctions in semi-specific PCR reactions. Size-selected DNA was sequenced with cycle paired-end runs on an Illumina GAII. Number of reads mapping to protein-coding sequences (CDS) were scored for each experiment.

Four different induced samples were examined: bloodstream-form cells grown for three days (BFd3) or six days (BFd6), insect/procyclic-form cells (PF), and cells induced throughout bloodstream growth and differentiation into procyclic forms (DIF). BFd3, BFd6, PF and DIF cultures were grown under inducing conditions (Tetracycline) for the equivalent of approximately 10, 20, 9 and 7+6 population doublings, respectively (~7 h for BF doubling, ~24 h for PF doubling).

Cells carrying RNAi target fragments that negatively impact fitness through dsRNA expression and RNAi-mediated ablation are relatively depleted as the population expands and these changes are reported by the depth of sequence coverage relative to the uninduced control (No Tet).

For further details, please refer the following manuscript: High-throughput phenotyping using parallel sequencing of RNA interference targets in the African trypanosome.

The following four searches return the lists of genes from this paper that show significant loss of fitness (Z-scores >= 3.3) for each of the stages tested in this experiment.

  • Blood form day 3
  • Blood form day 6
  • Procyclic form
  • Differentiation

This strategy shows loss of fitness in all four of the above samples. 1 The DIF sample involved RNAi induction throughout growth as bloodstream forms, differentiation and growth as procyclic forms, so that any gene required for growth in either life-cycle stage or for differentiation should register a loss-of-fitness in this sample.




Note: These data were re-analyzed as part of the loading protocol for TriTrypDB. RPKM values were computed for CDS sequences and annotated gene models (primarily just 5' UTR + CDS since only 10 genes have annotated 3' UTRs currently). Alsford et. al. used the CDS for their analyses since the annotation of UTRs is less reliable. Differences in the results can be clearly seen when comparing these two methods. For example by Tb927.8.2780. This gene was shown in Alsford et. al. to cause significant loss of fitness in all stages with there being zero reads for BFd3 and BFd6 while the entire gene model analysis shows there to be no decrease in reads in any stage. When we examined the coverage in Genome Browser for this region we found that all the alignments in this gene in blood form stages were to the 5' UTR and in fact, there is a predominant splice leader addition site for blood form stages between the alignments and the CDS, thus explaining the differences.
In the analysis carried out by Alsford et al., pseudogenes, genes annotated as "hypothetical unlikely", and genes belonging to the repetitive VSG, expression site associated (ESAG) or retrotransposon hotspot families were excluded. These genes may be returned by queries run on TriTrypDB.
searches.summary: Identify T.brucei  genes based on comparisons of RNAi target sequencing coverage at different life cycle stages.

searches.description:
Find genes based on predicted subcellular location from LOPIT analysis.

Protein location prediction was performed using a Bayesian generative classifier based on t-augmented Gaussian mixture models (TAGM) to probabilistically attribute proteins to subcellular niches using either maximum a posteriori prediction (TAGM-MAP) or Markov-chain Monte-Carlo (TAGM-MCMC) methods [1]. The method models each subcellular niche as a multivariate Gaussian distribution. To account for those proteins that are not adequately captured by the mixture of multivariate Gaussians, the model is augmented by a heavy-tailed multivariate Student's t-distribution representing an outlier component.

The data are shown as the joint probability of a protein belonging to the 26 defined subcellular niches (sums up to 1). In addition, the probability of a protein belonging to the outlier component of the classification model is also shown. A protein location can be inferred by examining the joint probability values to find the subcellular niche with the highest value and comparing it to the outlier probability.

IMPORTANT:

  1. TAGM-MAP and TAGM-MCMC use different methods to compute probabilities, and the reported probabilities are not the same.
  2. Always consider the outlier probability to make sure a given protein location prediction is reliable.
  3. In the case of TAGM-MAP, the joint probability is not the same as the allocation probability used to derive the final prediction; please, verify your results using the authors' website.
  4. Use TAGM-MCMC rather than TAGM-MAP to assess the uncertainty of location prediction and to look for proteins potentially occupying multiple locations.

[1] Crook, O.M., Mulvey, C.M., Kirk, P.D.W., Lilley, K.S., and Gatto, L. (2018). A Bayesian mixture modelling approach for spatial proteomics. PLOS Comput. Biol. 14, e1006516.
searches.summary: Find genes based on predicted subcellular location from LOPIT analysis.

searches.description:
Find genes whose proteins are predicted to have the amount of secondary-structure content (coil, strand or helix) that you specify.

The secondary-structure content is predicted by the PSIPRED program. The percent composition is computed by counting the amino acids in which one of the three calls (coil, strand or helix) is given the highest confidence, and dividing by the length of the protein. For example, a protein's percent helix content is the number of amino acids in which a helix call has the highest confidence, divided by the length of the protein.

Reference:
Jones DT. (1999) Protein secondary structure prediction
based on position-specific scoring matrices
J Mol Biol. 1999 Sep 17;292(2):195-202
searches.summary: Find genes whose proteins are predicted to have secondary-structure content (coil, strand or helix) that you specify.

Find genes that have been annotated as enzymes, i.e. that have been assigned an Enzyme Commission (EC) number.

Enzyme Commission numbers describe enzymes hierarchically by the class of reactions they catalyze. For help with obtaining EC numbers, try the ExPASy-ENZYME browser.

First select the Organism(s) you wish to query. The search will return genes from these organisms. Then choose the Source of Assignment. integrated EC numbers from several sources. EC assignments from more than one source may be queried in a single search. Genes returned by the search will have EC assignements from the Source that you select here.

Next indicate the EC Number or Term you wish to query. Begin typing an EC number or name to see a list of all possible EC categories that match what you have typed. Then choose an EC category from the list.

Alternatively, you can type in EC numbers or descriptions. You can use '-' or '*' in place of numbers to denote partial EC Numbers, for example, '2.7.7.-'. or *kinase*

searches.description:
Find genes that have evidence for protein-level expression from mass specrtometry-based proteomics experiments.

TriTrypDB maps peptides from proteomics experiments to a reference genome and allows you to search for genes based on that mapping. Expand the Experiment/Samples parameter to see a list of proteomics datasets integrated into TriTrypDB. The list is organized by:

  1. the organism that the peptides are mapped to
  2. the experiment name (model organism)
  3. the samples analyzed in the experiment
The stringency of the search can be adjusted using the "Minimum Number of Spectera / Sample" and "Minimum Number of Unique Peptide Sequences".
Minimum Number of Spectra / Sample:
Use this parameter to set a minimum for the number of mass spectra that must support a sample (all peptides) before a gene is returned for this sample (note that this number is the sum of spectra for all peptides / sample). This parameter can be considered a measure of protein abundance within a particular sample.

Minimum Number of Unique Peptide Sequences:
Use this parameter to define the number of unique peptides that must map to a gene before the gene is returned by the search. Although protein expression is confirmed with the mapping of one unique pepetide, requiring more than one peptide to map to a gene will ensure that false positives are not returned by the search. Note that the next parameter controls whether to apply this number per sample or across all samples.

Apply min # peptide sequences / sample OR across samples:
Select Per Sample to require that each sample meet this minimum number of unique peptide sequences. Selecting All will first union the unique peptides for all selected samples and this set will be used to meet the minimum number of unique peptide sequences.
searches.summary: Find genes that have evidence for protein-level expression from mass specrtometry-based proteomics experiments.

searches.description:
Find genes whose protein products show similarity to an epitope identified by the Immune Epitope Database and Analysis Resource (IEDB).

Epitopes are antigenic determinants recognized by the immune system's antibodies, B-cells or T-cells. The epitopes from the original Epitope Source Accession Number provided by IEDB are mapped to the corresponding gene identifiers in TriTrypDB.

Epitope sequences are mapped to genes in VEuPathDB using exact string matching or high quality BLAST similarity (percent identity >= 97%) between the GenBank proteins listed on IEDB and the proteins found in TriTrypDB. Confidence levels are assigned to each set of epitopes based on the quality of this mapping.

Find genes whose protein products are predicted to contain epitopes 
           identified by the Immune Epitope Database and Analysis Resource (IEDB).

searches.description:
Find genes that have BLAST similarity to your input sequence.

As of 3 Feb 2014, this search uses NCBI-BLAST to determine sequence similarity. Prior versions of the search used WU-BLAST. See the NCBI-BLAST help for more information.

First use the Target Data Type parameter to indicate the type of sequence (protein, transcript, genomic, etc.) that your Input Sequence should be BLASTed against. Then choose a BLAST Program to query your Input Sequence with and the Organism (genome) to use in your query.

Paste one Input Sequence in the text box. Only one sequence up to 31 Kb can be searched.

Default settings are indicated for the Expectation value, Maximum descriptions/alignments (V=B), and low complexity filter parameters.

BLAST Programs:
blastp compares an amino acid Input Sequence against a protein sequence database;
blastn compares a nucleotide Input Sequence against a nucleotide sequence database;

searches.description:
Find genes whose protein product contains a motif pattern that you specify.
First choose the Organism that you wish to query. Then define the motif to query by entering a Perl-style regular expression that defines the motif you want to find. Regular expressions are more powerful than PROSITE patterns.

For example, "CC6+RK" is a Perl style regular expression representing "two cysteines followed by one or more hydrophobic amino acids, followed by arginine and then lysine". This type of search pattern allows you to find sequences that may be less well conserved.

Another example is the pattern of the Pexel motif, which can be represented as "RXLX[EQD]", meaning "an arginine, then any amino acid, then a leucine, then any amino acid, then either an aspartic acid, a glutamic acid, or a glutamine". Note that the period (.) is used to search for any character, even a non-amino acid character like J or asterisk (*). Thus, the search pattern "S.T" could find "SWT" or "S*T" or "S-T".

For a description of how to create regular expressions, please see the Regular Expression Tutorial.

Find genes whose predicted protein contains a domain from the InterPro set of domain databases.

First choose the Organism(s) and Domain Database that you wish to query.

Then use either the 'Domain' or the 'Domain wildcard search' parameter to indicate the protein domain you wish to find.

When using the 'Specific Domain (s)' parameter, begin typing a domain name, accession or description, to see a list of all possible domains that match what you have typed. Then choose a domain name from the list. You can choose multiple domains using CTRL- or CMD-click when choosing the domains.

The domain matches to protein sequence are determined using the InterProScan program. To learn more about InterPro see the InterPro tutorial.

searches.description:
Find genes based on the Gene Ontology (GO) Term(s) or ID(s) assigned to them. GO annotations were either provided by the sequencing and annotation centers or inferred based on similarity to protein domains from the InterPro databases.

The Gene Ontology standardizes the representation of gene and gene product attributes across species and databases. The ontologies are a controlled vocabulary of terms for describing the molecular function, biological process and subcellular location of a gene product. This search returns genes with the GO Term or ID that you specify, as well as genes with terms that are specializations of your term (is-a). You may use '*' as a wild card character. For a list of GO terms, try the AmiGO browser.

When using the GO Subsets parameter selecting GO Slim generic will limit the search to GO terms that are part of the GO Slim generic ontology subset. To run on all available GO terms please select All GO terms.

When using the 'GO Term or GO ID' parameter, begin typing a GO Term or ID see a list of all possible GO categories that match what you have typed. Then choose a GO category from the list. You can choose multiple domains using CTRL- or CMD-click when choosing the domains.

When using the 'Free Text (use'*' for wildcard)' parameter, type the text term you wish to find and include an asterisk wildcard for ambiguous portions of your text term. (*ase, kin*, *kinase*) The search will query for all terms or IDs whose names, accessions or descriptions contain your text.

searches.description:
Find genes that have a specified orthology-based phylogenetic profile. The phylogenetic profile of a gene is a series of "present" or "absent" calls, reflecting the inclusion of a gene in ortholog groups determined by the OrthoMCL algorithm.

The OrthoMCL algorithm clusters proteins into ortholog groups based on BLAST similarity across at least 150 genomes that span the tree of life. The ortholog groups document protein similarity across many species. Mapping ortholog groups onto the phyletic tree of life provides a framework for correlating protein similarity across species. The other species that are included in that gene's ortholog group can be thought of as a phylogenetic profile.

Use this search to define a pattern across those ortholog groups, and find genes that match that pattern. The pattern is a specification, for each species, of "include", "exclude", or "no constraints." Click on the radio button next to a species to toggle through the three states. A means "include", an means "exclude" and means "no constraints".

For example, to find genes that are present in Apicomplexa but not in humans, click on Apicomplexa until you see a and click on Homo sapiens until you see an .
searches.summary: Find genes that have an orthology-based phylogenetic profile that you specify.

searches.description:
Find genes by searching text annotations. The search compares your term against the text in the fields you specify, returning genes that have a match.

Select the Organism(s) you wish to query and enter your text term. Surround your text term with quotation marks to find exact phrase matches. For example, searching "ABC transporter" will match the exact phrase 'ABC transporter', whereas searching ABC transporter will match ABC and/or transporter. Use an asterisk (*) as a wild card character when looking for plural or compound words. For example, to find all compound words that start with phospho (ie. phosphodiesterase), type phospho* in the search window.

Hints: The search is similar to Google -- if you enter multiple words, genes that match more of those words will have a better score than those that match fewer of the words. If the words are found close together, that also improves the score. Higher scores appear at the top of your result list.

Looking for a list of genes?: If you need to query for a list of gene and you have each gene's ID, use the Identify Genes based on List of IDs search categorized under Genes, Annotation curation and identifiers, List of IDs.

Note about non-relevant results: Depending on how you configure it, this text search may return "non-relevant" genes (false positives). The search mechanically matches the term you supply against the Fields that you choose. The presence of your term in that field does not necessarily mean that the term actually describes the gene. The term may be mentioned in that field for less relevant reasons. To work around this, please carefully choose the Fields you want to search, and then, before drawing any conclusions, review the reference to your term in all matched fields in the gene page to confirm the meaning of its mention. The "Gene product" field is the most stringent and is unlikely to return false positives.

searches.description:
Find genes within a given distance from a telomere.

Because telomere sequences are repetitive, they are not included in genome sequences. This search uses the start and end positions of chromosomes as the location of telomeres. When defining parameters for this search, please take into account that the actual location of the telomere is near the end of the chromosome.

searches.description:
Find genes with a copy number in a resequenced strain that is within a range that you specify.

Whole genome resequencing data was used to estimate each gene's copy number in resequenced strains. This search returns genes that are present at copy numbers (haploid number or gene dose) within a range that you specify.

You have the choice between two different metrics for defining copy number: haploid number or gene dose. Haploid number is the number of genes on an individual chromosome. Gene dose is the total number of genes in an organism, accounting for copy number of the chromosome. For example, a single-copy gene in a diploid organism has a haploid number of 1 and a gene dose of 2. You can choose to search for genes where at least one of your selected isolates meets your cutoff criteria for the chosen metric (By Strain/Sample), or where the median of the chosen metric across all the selected isolates meets the cutoff (Median of Selected Strains/Samples)

Begin by choosing an Organism (reference genome) and one or more resequenced isolates. Choose whether you want to apply your search criteris to individual samples or to the median of your chosen samples. Then choose your Metric, Operator and Copy Number, and initiate the search by clicking the GET ANSWER button. Genes returned by the search will have a copy number based on your chosen metric within the range that you specified. For example, searching with the haploid number equal to 4 will return genes with 4 copies on a chromosome.
searches.summary: Find genes based on the number of copies in resequenced strains

searches.description:
Find genes by comparing the gene copy number in one or more resequenced strains to its copy number in the reference genome.

Whole genome resequencing was used to estimate each gene's copy number in resequenced strains. This search compares the estimated copy number of a gene in the resequenced strain with the copy number in the reference annotation. The copy number in the reference annotation is calculated as the number of genes that are both on the same chromosome and in the same ortholog group as the gene of interest. We infer that these genes have arisen as a result of tandem duplication of a common ancestor.

In this search, the metric for copy number is the haploid number, which is the number of copies of a gene on a single chromosome.

Begin by choosing an Organism (reference genome), and one or more resequenced strains, then choose how you want to compare the resequenced strains to the reference. You can search for genes where the estimated copy number in the resequenced strains is greater than or equal to, equal to, or less than or equal to the number of copies in the reference genome. You can choose to search for genes where at least one of your selected strains meets your chosen criteria (By Strain/Sample), or where the median across all your selected strains meets the criteria (Median of Selected Strains/Samples) After making your selections, initiate the search by clicking on the GET ANSWER button.

Be cautious using the less than or equal to operator, because regions which do not sequence well may appear to have reductions in gene copy number.

Find genes by comparing the gene copy number in the resequenced strain to its copy 
                 number in the reference genome.

searches.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment. Differential expression is based on the number of unique reads mapped to each gene. First choose an Experiment since the available samples may change between experiments. If there is only one Experiment shown, this field will be selected for you.

Set the directionality of change in expression that you would like to see in the genes returned by this search. Choose to search for up-regulated, down-regulated, or up- and down-regulated genes.

Use the Fold Change >= parameter to set the cutoff for the change in expression for the genes returned by the search.

Choose the samples that you wish to compare. You may choose one or more samples for the reference and comparison. Fold change is calculated between your chosen reference and comparison samples and no statistical analysis is applied. For up-regulated genes the comparison/reference ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For down-regulated genes the reference/comparison ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference. There is an option to search for both up- and down- regulated genes in one query.

After selecting samples you have the option to perform the fold change calulation with the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further.
searches.summary: Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment.

searches.displayName: T. brucei brucei TREU927 Procyclic and bloodstream form transcriptomes and ribosome profiling RNA-Seq (fold change)
searches.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment. Differential expression is based on the number of unique reads mapped to each gene. First choose an Experiment since the available samples may change between experiments. If there is only one Experiment shown, this field will be selected for you.

Set the directionality of change in expression that you would like to see in the genes returned by this search. Choose to search for up-regulated, down-regulated, or up- and down-regulated genes.

Use the Fold Change >= parameter to set the cutoff for the change in expression for the genes returned by the search.

Choose the samples that you wish to compare. You may choose one or more samples for the reference and comparison. Fold change is calculated between your chosen reference and comparison samples and no statistical analysis is applied. For up-regulated genes the comparison/reference ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For down-regulated genes the reference/comparison ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference. There is an option to search for both up- and down- regulated genes in one query.

After selecting samples you have the option to perform the fold change calulation with the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further.
searches.summary: Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment.

searches.displayName: T. brucei brucei TREU927 Procyclic and bloodstream form mRNA transcriptome and ribosome profiling RNA-Seq (Differential Expression)
searches.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment as determined by DESeq analysis. Differential expression is based on the number of unique reads for each gene. Please choose experiment. If only one "Experiment" is shown, this field will be selected for you.

Please choose a reference and a comparator sample. You can choose the directionality and the magnitude of the difference by setting both fold change and adjusted p values. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 and a adjusted p value cut off of 0.1 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference with a adjusted p value of 0.1 or less.

Please note only those samples from your choosen experiment that have at least 2 replicates are shown.
searches.summary: Find genes which are determined to be differentially expressed by DESeq analysis in an RNA-Seq experiment.

searches.displayName: T. brucei brucei TREU927 T. brucei procyclic cell cycle proteome Proteomics (fold change)
searches.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in a Proteomics experiment. First choose an experiment as the available samples may change. If only one "Experiment" is shown, this field will be selected for you.

After selecting samples you have the option to take the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further. Finally, you can choose the directionality and the magnitude of the difference. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference.

Any values less than the floor of 0.01 are raised to 0.01 to compute the fold difference.
searches.summary: Find genes which are differentially expressed in a Proteomics experiment.

searches.displayName: L. donovani BPK282A1 Visceral vs cutaneous isolate transcriptomes changes in sense and antisense transcripts
searches.shortDisplayName: Ld visce vs cutaneous RNA-Seq (sense antisense)
searches.description:
Find genes that exhibit simultaneous changes in sense and antisense transcripts in the Comparison sample relative to the Reference Sample. For example, you could look for genes showing increasing antisense transcripts and decreasing sense transcripts, as might occur when antisense transcription suppresses sense transcription. The search will perform all pairwise comparisons between the chosen Comparison samples and the chosen Reference samples. Below is an example where there is an increase in antisense transcripts and a decrease in sense transcripts in the Comparison sample:



An example of the TPM data for a gene is shown below. You can select the direction and the magnitude of change for the sense and antisense transcripts.



The results page lists the genes, along with each pair of samples (Reference->Comparison), that meet the criteria. The results page also shows a graph depicting all pairwise fold-changes in antisense and sense transcripts that is useful in identifying which samples meet the criteria that you selected AND whether this pattern is observed across all samples.



Each point shows the sense fold-change and the antisense fold-change between a pair of samples. A point on the red dotted diagonal line represents a pair of samples where the antisense fold-change and the sense fold-change are the same. Sample pairs that meet the fold-change critera are represented by points located within the corner of the graph that is closed off with a vertical and a horizontal red dotted line. (Note that some pairs meet the fold-change criteria but do not meet the change in antisense fraction, which is an advanced parameter. If you want to identify more genes, then you should decrease the value of this parameter.) On the Results page, you can click on the graph to open a new browser window containing an enlarged graph. The enlarged graph can be moused-over to show which sample comparison is represented by each point.
searches.summary: Find genes with specific patterns of sense and antisense transcripts, using evidence from strand-specific RNA-Seq data

searches.displayName: T. brucei brucei TREU927 Transcriptome of T. brucei rhodesiense from human, rodent, culture changes in sense and antisense transcripts
searches.shortDisplayName: Transcriptome of T. brucei rhodesiense from human, rodent, culture (sense antisense)
searches.description:
Find genes that exhibit simultaneous changes in sense and antisense transcripts in the Comparison sample relative to the Reference Sample. For example, you could look for genes showing increasing antisense transcripts and decreasing sense transcripts, as might occur when antisense transcription suppresses sense transcription. The search will perform all pairwise comparisons between the chosen Comparison samples and the chosen Reference samples. Below is an example where there is an increase in antisense transcripts and a decrease in sense transcripts in the Comparison sample:



An example of the TPM data for a gene is shown below. You can select the direction and the magnitude of change for the sense and antisense transcripts.



The results page lists the genes, along with each pair of samples (Reference->Comparison), that meet the criteria. The results page also shows a graph depicting all pairwise fold-changes in antisense and sense transcripts that is useful in identifying which samples meet the criteria that you selected AND whether this pattern is observed across all samples.



Each point shows the sense fold-change and the antisense fold-change between a pair of samples. A point on the red dotted diagonal line represents a pair of samples where the antisense fold-change and the sense fold-change are the same. Sample pairs that meet the fold-change critera are represented by points located within the corner of the graph that is closed off with a vertical and a horizontal red dotted line. (Note that some pairs meet the fold-change criteria but do not meet the change in antisense fraction, which is an advanced parameter. If you want to identify more genes, then you should decrease the value of this parameter.) On the Results page, you can click on the graph to open a new browser window containing an enlarged graph. The enlarged graph can be moused-over to show which sample comparison is represented by each point.

searches.displayName: T. cruzi Dm28c 2018 T cruzi life stages transcriptomes aligned to T cruzi Dm28c 2018 changes in sense and antisense transcripts
searches.description:
Find genes that exhibit simultaneous changes in sense and antisense transcripts in the Comparison sample relative to the Reference Sample. For example, you could look for genes showing increasing antisense transcripts and decreasing sense transcripts, as might occur when antisense transcription suppresses sense transcription. The search will perform all pairwise comparisons between the chosen Comparison samples and the chosen Reference samples. Below is an example where there is an increase in antisense transcripts and a decrease in sense transcripts in the Comparison sample:



An example of the TPM data for a gene is shown below. You can select the direction and the magnitude of change for the sense and antisense transcripts.



The results page lists the genes, along with each pair of samples (Reference->Comparison), that meet the criteria. The results page also shows a graph depicting all pairwise fold-changes in antisense and sense transcripts that is useful in identifying which samples meet the criteria that you selected AND whether this pattern is observed across all samples.



Each point shows the sense fold-change and the antisense fold-change between a pair of samples. A point on the red dotted diagonal line represents a pair of samples where the antisense fold-change and the sense fold-change are the same. Sample pairs that meet the fold-change critera are represented by points located within the corner of the graph that is closed off with a vertical and a horizontal red dotted line. (Note that some pairs meet the fold-change criteria but do not meet the change in antisense fraction, which is an advanced parameter. If you want to identify more genes, then you should decrease the value of this parameter.) On the Results page, you can click on the graph to open a new browser window containing an enlarged graph. The enlarged graph can be moused-over to show which sample comparison is represented by each point.
searches.summary: Find genes with specific patterns of sense and antisense transcripts, using evidence from strand-specific RNA-Seq data

searches.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an RNA-Seq experiment. First choose an experiment as the available samples may change. If only one "Experiment" is shown, this field will be selected for you.

After selecting samples you have the option to take the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further. Finally, you can choose the directionality and the magnitude of the difference. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference.

searches.description:
Find the TriTrypDB genes that are orthologs (or paralogs) of the genes in a search result. The typical use of this query is to begin by having an interesting result in a strategy. Then, use this search to find orthologs of those genes in a species that may not be annotated with the data from your original result. In general, use this search to transform sets of genes from one species to others.

Ortholog groups were generated from more than 100 species using OrthoMCL as described in Li L, Stoeckert CJ Jr, Roos DS. OrthoMCL: identification of ortholog groups for eukaryotic genomes. Genome Res. 2003 13:2178-89. The OrthoMCL DB site is described in Chen F. Mackey AJ. Stoeckert CJ Jr. Roos DS. OrthoMCL-DB: querying a comprehensive multi-species collection of ortholog groups. NAR. 34(Database issue):D363-8.

attributes.name: ai_expression
attributes.help: This experimental feature uses AI to help interpret the gene's expression data shown in the "Transcript Expression" section further down the page. First, the AI analyzes each individual experiment using its numeric data and metadata to generate a one-sentence summary and an estimated biological relevance score. Then, those per-experiment summaries are grouped into topics to highlight common expression patterns across experiments.

searches.displayName: Text (search product name, notes, submitter etc.)
searches.description:
Find popset sequences by searching text annotations. The search compares your term against the text in the fields you specify, returning popset sequences that have a match. Remember to select your species/organism of interest (more than one species may be selected).

The search is similar to Google: if you enter multiple words, popset sequences that match more of those words will have a better score than those that match fewer of the words. If the words are found close together, that also improves the score. You may use '*' as a wild card character.

Note about non-relevant results: Depending on how you configure it, this text search may return "non-relevant" popset sequences (false positives). The search mechanically matches the term you supply against the fields described in the Fields parameter. The presence of your term in that field does not necessarily mean that the term actually describes the popset. The term may be mentioned in that field for less relevant reasons. To work around this, please choose the Fields you want to search carefully, and then, before drawing any conclusions, review the reference to your term in all matched fields in the popset page to confirm the meaning of its mention.
searches.summary: Find popset sequences with a text search against their reference or gene info.

searches.description:
Find genomic sequences or chromosomes based on their estimated copy number in resequenced strains.

Whole genome resequencing data was used to estimate the copy number (ploidy) of genomic sequences in the resequenced strains. This search returns genomic sequences or chromosomes with an estimated copy number greater than or equal to a value that you specify in at least one of the chosen samples. Begin by choosing an Organism (reference genome). Next choose one or more strains or samples that have been mapped against the chosen reference. Choose whether you want to search for genomic sequences where the group median for the selection strains/samples meets the Copy Number criteria (Median) or whether you want at least one of the strains/samples in the group to meet the Copy Number criteria (By Sample). Then enter a value for Copy Number and initiate the search by clicking the GET ANSWER button.

Genomic sequences returned by the search will have either have a median estimated copy number greater than or equal to the value you entered for the Copy Number across the selected strains/samples, or will have an estimated copy number greater than or equal to the value you entered for the Copy Number in at least one of the selected strains/samples. For example, to find supernumerary chromosomes in a diploid organism, search for genomic sequences where the Copy Number is >= 3.
searches.summary: Find genomic sequences or chromosomes based on the number of copies in the genome.

searches.displayName: Differences Within a Group of Isolates
searches.description:
This search analyzes whole genome sequencing data from a group of isolates to find SNPs associated with the group.

Each isolate's sequencing reads are aligned to the reference genome (Organism) and SNPs are recorded for each isolate based on the Read Frequency Threshold. Then, scanning SNP locations across the group of isolates, SNPs are returned by the search if the Minor Allele Frequency and the Percent Isolates with a base call are met.

Organism: Choosing an Organism.
The Organism parameter defines the species of the parasite isolates and the genome in which the SNPs are determined. Choosing an Organism focuses the Isolates parameter to the list of isolates of that organism, thus changing the subset of isolates available when forming your group.

Isolates: Choosing the isolate group.
Isolate sequences are accompanied by information about the sequencing data set - metadata such as the clinical phenotype of the host or the location collected. By default, the isolate group includes all isolates from the Organism you chose. You have the option to limit the group of isolates based on metadata characteristics. For example, you can find SNPs for isolates collected from a certain geographic location. To do this, click a metadata category (Country) on the left and choose your desired metadata characteristic (e.g. Peru) on the right. Multiple metadata categories and characteristics can be chosen when defining your group. Not all isolate data sets have the same metadata. A running total of your selections is displayed above the metadata filter.

Read Frequency Threshold: Calling SNPs for each isolate in your group.
Each isolate's sequencing reads are aligned to a reference genome (Organism) and then each nucleotide position with 5 or more aligned reads is examined. A base call is made if the aligned reads meet your Read Frequency Threshold. For example, Isolate X has 10 aligned reads at nucleotide position 1600. If 6 reads are G and 4 reads are A, the read frequency is 60% for the G call and 40% for A. Running this search with the Read Frequency Threshold set to 80% will prevent a base call and consequently exclude Isolate X when returning SNPs for nucleotide position 1600. Running the search with the Read Frequency Threshold set to 60% will bring back a G for this isolate and a 40% threshold will return two calls (both G and A) at this position. The parameter lets you control the quality of the sequencing data and the confidence of the SNP calls. Read Frequency Threshold is a particularly important parameter when dealing with diploid (or aneuploid) organisms since a read frequency of ~50% is expected for heterozygous SNPs.



The SNPs returned by this search are found by aligning the isolates (with SNPs recorded as described above) and applying 2 parameters across the group of isolates: Percent isolates with a base call and Minor allele frequency.

Percent isolates with a base call: Parameter 1 for calling SNPs across your isolate group
Sometimes an isolate does not have a base call at a certain nucleotide position because the Read Frequency Threshold was not met or because there were less than 5 aligned sequencing reads for that nucleotide position. In this case, a SNP can be returned by the search based on a subset of your isolate group. The 'Percent isolates with a base call' parameter defines the fraction of isolates that must have a base call before a SNP is returned for that nucleotide position. The default setting for this parameter is 80% or 8 out of 10 isolates in your group must have a base call for a SNP to be returned by the search. The higher this parameter, the more likely the SNP is to be high quality as regions difficult to align or difficult to sequence will tend to have a lower percentage of calls since the coverage and/or quality will be lower in that region.

Minor allele frequency: Parameter 2 for calling SNPs across your isolate group.
The minor allele frequency refers to the least common base call for a single nucleotide position across all isolates. The default setting for this parameter is 0% and returns all SNPs - instances where at least one isolate has a base call that differs from reference. Increase the Minor allele frequency to ensure that SNPs returned by the search are shared by a larger percentage of isolates in your group.

searches.description:
This search compares whole genome sequencing data from two groups of isolates to find SNPs that differ between the two groups.

Each isolate's sequencing reads are aligned to the reference genome (Organism) and SNPs are recorded for each isolate based on the Read Frequency Threshold. Then, scanning SNP locations across isolates in Set A and B separately, SNPs within each set are recorded if they meet the major allele frequency and percent isolates with a base call. SNPs returned by the search are ones that differ between Isolate Set A and B.

Organism: Choosing an Organism.
The Organism parameter defines the species of the parasite isolates and the genome in which the SNPs are determined. Choosing an Organism focuses the Isolates parameter to the list of isolates of that organism, thus changing the subset of isolates available when forming your group.

Isolates: Choosing isolate Set A and B.
Isolate sequences are accompanied by information about the sequencing data set - metadata such as the clinical phenotype of the host or the location collected. By default, the isolate group includes all isolates from the Organism you chose. You have the option to limit the group of isolates based on metadata characteristics. For example, you can find SNPs for isolates collected from a certain geographic location. To do this, click a metadata category (Country) on the left and choose your desired metadata characteristic (e.g. Peru) on the right. Multiple metadata categories and characteristics can be chosen when defining your group. Not all isolate data sets have the same metadata. A running total of your selections is displayed above the metadata filter.

Read Frequency Threshold: Calling SNPs for each isolate in a set.
Each isolate's sequencing reads are aligned to a reference genome (Organism) and then each nucleotide position with 5 or more aligned reads is examined. A base call is made if the aligned reads meet your Read Frequency Threshold. For example, Isolate X has 10 aligned reads at nucleotide position 1600. If 6 reads are G and 4 reads are A, the read frequency is 60% for the G call and 40% for A. Running this search with the Read Frequency Threshold set to 80% will prevent a base call and consequently exclude Isolate X when returning SNPs for nucleotide position 1600. Running the search with the Read Frequency Threshold set to 60% will bring back a G for this isolate and a 40% threshold will return two calls (both G and A) at this position. The parameter lets you control the quality of the sequencing data and the confidence of the SNP calls. Read Frequency Threshold is a particularly important parameter when dealing with diploid (or aneuploid) organisms since a read frequency of ~50% is expected for heterozygous SNPs.



The SNPs returned by this search are found by comparing SNPs from Set A Isolates with those from Set B. SNPs are recorded for each set by aligning the isolates in each set (with isolate specific SNPs recorded as described above for read frequency threshold) and applying 2 parameters across the isolate sets: Percent isolates with a base call and Major allele frequency. SNPs returned by the search have different base call between group A isolates and group B isolates.

Percent isolates with a base call: Parameter 1 for recording SNPs in isolate sets
Sometimes an isolate does not have a base call at a certain nucleotide position because the Read Frequency Threshold was not met or because there were less than 5 aligned sequencing reads for that nucleotide position. In this case, a SNP can be returned by the search based on a subset of your isolate group. The 'Percent isolates with a base call' parameter defines the fraction of isolates that must have a base call before a SNP is recorded for that nucleotide position. The default setting for this parameter is 80% or 8 out of 10 isolates in your set must have a base call for a SNP to be recorded for the set of isolates.

Major Allele Frequency: Parameter 2 for recording SNPs in isolate sets
The major allele frequency is the frequency of the most common SNP across the isolates in a Set. The default setting for this parameter is 80%. SNPs returned by the two groups search will have a different major allele call between Set A and Set B. See image below.

If a user logs in more than once during the time period, we only count once for that user.

transcript.displayName: High-Throughput Phenotyping
transcript.description:
Identify T. brucei genes based on comparisons of RNAi target sequencing coverage at different life cycle stages. Genes returned by this search have coverage (RPKM) values in Comparison Sample(s) that is less than that of the Uninduced Control.

In this experiment an RNAi plasmid library, containing randomly sheared genomic fragments was used to create an inducible library in bloodstream form T. brucei. After transfection, the library was grown under non-inducing and inducing conditions and genomic DNA was isolated from surviving populations. Adapter-ligated sequencing libraries were prepared from each genomic DNA sample and used to amplify DNA fragments containing RNAi cassette-insert junctions in semi-specific PCR reactions. Size-selected DNA was sequenced with cycle paired-end runs on an Illumina GAII. Number of reads mapping to protein-coding sequences (CDS) were scored for each experiment.

Four different induced samples were examined: bloodstream-form cells grown for three days (BFd3) or six days (BFd6), insect/procyclic-form cells (PF), and cells induced throughout bloodstream growth and differentiation into procyclic forms (DIF). BFd3, BFd6, PF and DIF cultures were grown under inducing conditions (Tetracycline) for the equivalent of approximately 10, 20, 9 and 7+6 population doublings, respectively (~7 h for BF doubling, ~24 h for PF doubling).

Cells carrying RNAi target fragments that negatively impact fitness through dsRNA expression and RNAi-mediated ablation are relatively depleted as the population expands and these changes are reported by the depth of sequence coverage relative to the uninduced control (No Tet).

For further details, please refer the following manuscript: High-throughput phenotyping using parallel sequencing of RNA interference targets in the African trypanosome.

The following four searches return the lists of genes from this paper that show significant loss of fitness (Z-scores >= 3.3) for each of the stages tested in this experiment.

  • Blood form day 3
  • Blood form day 6
  • Procyclic form
  • Differentiation

This strategy shows loss of fitness in all four of the above samples. 1 The DIF sample involved RNAi induction throughout growth as bloodstream forms, differentiation and growth as procyclic forms, so that any gene required for growth in either life-cycle stage or for differentiation should register a loss-of-fitness in this sample.




Note: These data were re-analyzed as part of the loading protocol for TriTrypDB. RPKM values were computed for CDS sequences and annotated gene models (primarily just 5' UTR + CDS since only 10 genes have annotated 3' UTRs currently). Alsford et. al. used the CDS for their analyses since the annotation of UTRs is less reliable. Differences in the results can be clearly seen when comparing these two methods. For example by Tb927.8.2780. This gene was shown in Alsford et. al. to cause significant loss of fitness in all stages with there being zero reads for BFd3 and BFd6 while the entire gene model analysis shows there to be no decrease in reads in any stage. When we examined the coverage in Genome Browser for this region we found that all the alignments in this gene in blood form stages were to the 5' UTR and in fact, there is a predominant splice leader addition site for blood form stages between the alignments and the CDS, thus explaining the differences.
In the analysis carried out by Alsford et al., pseudogenes, genes annotated as "hypothetical unlikely", and genes belonging to the repetitive VSG, expression site associated (ESAG) or retrotransposon hotspot families were excluded. These genes may be returned by queries run on TriTrypDB.
transcript.summary: Identify T.brucei  genes based on comparisons of RNAi target sequencing coverage at different life cycle stages.

transcript.displayName: Genomic Location
transcript.description:
Find genes that are located within a specified genomic region. Use either the Chromosome Tab or Sequence ID Tab to define the genomic location you wish to query. The search returns all genes found within your specified genomic location.

Chromosome Tab:
First select the Organism and Chromosome that you want to query. Then indicate the boundaries of the genomic location by entering the Start and End nucleotide coordinates of your region. Choosing Start=1 and End=0 will retrieve all genes on the chromosome.

Sequence ID Tab:
First enter the Genomic Sequence ID of the contig or chromosome that you want to query. Example genomic sequence IDs are: LmjF.36, LbrM.02, TcChr10-S, TvY486_11. Then indicate the boundaries of the genomic location by entering the Start and End nucleotide coordinates of your region. Choosing Start=1 and End=0 will retrieve all genes on the genomic sequence.
transcript.summary: Find genes within a given genomic region such as a chromosome, scaffold or supercontig.

transcript.displayName: Localization by LOPIT Mass Spec
transcript.description:
Find genes based on predicted subcellular location from LOPIT analysis.

Protein location prediction was performed using a Bayesian generative classifier based on t-augmented Gaussian mixture models (TAGM) to probabilistically attribute proteins to subcellular niches using either maximum a posteriori prediction (TAGM-MAP) or Markov-chain Monte-Carlo (TAGM-MCMC) methods [1]. The method models each subcellular niche as a multivariate Gaussian distribution. To account for those proteins that are not adequately captured by the mixture of multivariate Gaussians, the model is augmented by a heavy-tailed multivariate Student's t-distribution representing an outlier component.

The data are shown as the joint probability of a protein belonging to the 26 defined subcellular niches (sums up to 1). In addition, the probability of a protein belonging to the outlier component of the classification model is also shown. A protein location can be inferred by examining the joint probability values to find the subcellular niche with the highest value and comparing it to the outlier probability.

IMPORTANT:

  1. TAGM-MAP and TAGM-MCMC use different methods to compute probabilities, and the reported probabilities are not the same.
  2. Always consider the outlier probability to make sure a given protein location prediction is reliable.
  3. In the case of TAGM-MAP, the joint probability is not the same as the allocation probability used to derive the final prediction; please, verify your results using the authors' website.
  4. Use TAGM-MCMC rather than TAGM-MAP to assess the uncertainty of location prediction and to look for proteins potentially occupying multiple locations.

[1] Crook, O.M., Mulvey, C.M., Kirk, P.D.W., Lilley, K.S., and Gatto, L. (2018). A Bayesian mixture modelling approach for spatial proteomics. PLOS Comput. Biol. 14, e1006516.
transcript.summary: Find genes based on predicted subcellular location from LOPIT analysis.

transcript.displayName: Protein Secondary Structure
transcript.description:
Find genes whose proteins are predicted to have the amount of secondary-structure content (coil, strand or helix) that you specify.

The secondary-structure content is predicted by the PSIPRED program. The percent composition is computed by counting the amino acids in which one of the three calls (coil, strand or helix) is given the highest confidence, and dividing by the length of the protein. For example, a protein's percent helix content is the number of amino acids in which a helix call has the highest confidence, divided by the length of the protein.

Reference:
Jones DT. (1999) Protein secondary structure prediction
based on position-specific scoring matrices
J Mol Biol. 1999 Sep 17;292(2):195-202
transcript.summary: Find genes whose proteins are predicted to have secondary-structure content (coil, strand or helix) that you specify.

transcript.displayName: EC Number
transcript.description:
Find genes that have been annotated as enzymes, i.e. that have been assigned an Enzyme Commission (EC) number.

Enzyme Commission numbers describe enzymes hierarchically by the class of reactions they catalyze. For help with obtaining EC numbers, try the ExPASy-ENZYME browser.

First select the Organism(s) you wish to query. The search will return genes from these organisms. Then choose the Source of Assignment. integrated EC numbers from several sources. EC assignments from more than one source may be queried in a single search. Genes returned by the search will have EC assignements from the Source that you select here.

Next indicate the EC Number or Term you wish to query. Begin typing an EC number or name to see a list of all possible EC categories that match what you have typed. Then choose an EC category from the list.

Alternatively, you can type in EC numbers or descriptions. You can use '-' or '*' in place of numbers to denote partial EC Numbers, for example, '2.7.7.-'. or *kinase*
transcript.summary: Find genes that have been annotated as enzymes, i.e, that have been assigned an Enzyme Commission (EC) number.

transcript.displayName: Mass Spec. Evidence
transcript.description:
Find genes that have evidence for protein-level expression from mass specrtometry-based proteomics experiments.

TriTrypDB maps peptides from proteomics experiments to a reference genome and allows you to search for genes based on that mapping. Expand the Experiment/Samples parameter to see a list of proteomics datasets integrated into TriTrypDB. The list is organized by:

  1. the organism that the peptides are mapped to
  2. the experiment name (model organism)
  3. the samples analyzed in the experiment
The stringency of the search can be adjusted using the "Minimum Number of Spectera / Sample" and "Minimum Number of Unique Peptide Sequences".
Minimum Number of Spectra / Sample:
Use this parameter to set a minimum for the number of mass spectra that must support a sample (all peptides) before a gene is returned for this sample (note that this number is the sum of spectra for all peptides / sample). This parameter can be considered a measure of protein abundance within a particular sample.

Minimum Number of Unique Peptide Sequences:
Use this parameter to define the number of unique peptides that must map to a gene before the gene is returned by the search. Although protein expression is confirmed with the mapping of one unique pepetide, requiring more than one peptide to map to a gene will ensure that false positives are not returned by the search. Note that the next parameter controls whether to apply this number per sample or across all samples.

Apply min # peptide sequences / sample OR across samples:
Select Per Sample to require that each sample meet this minimum number of unique peptide sequences. Selecting All will first union the unique peptides for all selected samples and this set will be used to meet the minimum number of unique peptide sequences.
transcript.summary: Find genes that have evidence for protein-level expression from mass specrtometry-based proteomics experiments.

transcript.displayName: Post-Translational Modification
transcript.description:

transcript.description:

Epitopes are antigenic determinants recognized by the immune system's antibodies, B-cells or T-cells. The epitopes from the original Epitope Source Accession Number provided by IEDB are mapped to the corresponding gene identifiers in TriTrypDB.

Epitope sequences are mapped to genes in VEuPathDB using exact string matching or high quality BLAST similarity (percent identity >= 97%) between the GenBank proteins listed on IEDB and the proteins found in TriTrypDB. transcript.displayName: BLAST
transcript.description:
Find genes that have BLAST similarity to your input sequence.

As of 3 Feb 2014, this search uses NCBI-BLAST to determine sequence similarity. Prior versions of the search used WU-BLAST. See the NCBI-BLAST help for more information.

First use the Target Data Type parameter to indicate the type of sequence (protein, transcript, genomic, etc.) that your Input Sequence should be BLASTed against. Then choose a BLAST Program to query your Input Sequence with and the Organism (genome) to use in your query.

Paste one Input Sequence in the text box. Only one sequence up to 31 Kb can be searched.

Default settings are indicated for the Expectation value, Maximum descriptions/alignments (V=B), and low complexity filter parameters.

BLAST Programs:
blastp compares an amino acid Input Sequence against a protein sequence database;
blastn compares a nucleotide Input Sequence against a nucleotide sequence database;
blastx compares the six-frame conceptual translation products of a nucleotide Input Sequence (both strands) against a protein sequence database;
tblastn compares a protein Input Sequence against a nucleotide sequence database dynamically translated in all six reading frames (both strands);
tblastx compares the six-frame translations of a nucleotide Input Sequence against the six-frame translations of a nucleotide sequence database.
transcript.summary: Find genes that have BLAST similarity to your input sequence.

transcript.displayName: Protein Motif Pattern
transcript.description:
Find genes whose protein product contains a motif pattern that you specify.
First choose the Organism that you wish to query. Then define the motif to query by entering a Perl-style regular expression that defines the motif you want to find. Regular expressions are more powerful than PROSITE patterns.

For example, "CC6+RK" is a Perl style regular expression representing "two cysteines followed by one or more hydrophobic amino acids, followed by arginine and then lysine". This type of search pattern allows you to find sequences that may be less well conserved.

Another example is the pattern of the Pexel motif, which can be represented as "RXLX[EQD]", meaning "an arginine, then any amino acid, then a leucine, then any amino acid, then either an aspartic acid, a glutamic acid, or a glutamine". Note that the period (.) is used to search for any character, even a non-amino acid character like J or asterisk (*). Thus, the search pattern "S.T" could find "SWT" or "S*T" or "S-T".

For a description of how to create regular expressions, please see the Regular Expression Tutorial.

The following codes can be used to represent classes of amino acids.

transcript.description:
Find genes whose predicted protein contains a domain from the InterPro set of domain databases.

First choose the Organism(s) and Domain Database that you wish to query.

Then use either the 'Domain' or the 'Domain wildcard search' parameter to indicate the protein domain you wish to find.

When using the 'Specific Domain (s)' parameter, begin typing a domain name, accession or description, to see a list of all possible domains that match what you have typed. Then choose a domain name from the list. You can choose multiple domains using CTRL- or CMD-click when choosing the domains.

When using the 'Free Text (use'*' for wildcard)' parameter, type the text term you wish to find, including an asterisk wildcard for ambiguous portions of your text term. (*ase, kin*, *kinase*) The search will query for all domains whose names, accessions or descriptions contain your text.

The domain matches to protein sequence are determined using the InterProScan program. To learn more about InterPro see the InterPro tutorial.

transcript.description:
Find genes based on the Gene Ontology (GO) Term(s) or ID(s) assigned to them. GO annotations were either provided by the sequencing and annotation centers or inferred based on similarity to protein domains from the InterPro databases.

The Gene Ontology standardizes the representation of gene and gene product attributes across species and databases. The ontologies are a controlled vocabulary of terms for describing the molecular function, biological process and subcellular location of a gene product. This search returns genes with the GO Term or ID that you specify, as well as genes with terms that are specializations of your term (is-a). You may use '*' as a wild card character. For a list of GO terms, try the AmiGO browser.

When using the GO Subsets parameter selecting GO Slim generic will limit the search to GO terms that are part of the GO Slim generic ontology subset. To run on all available GO terms please select All GO terms.

When using the 'GO Term or GO ID' parameter, begin typing a GO Term or ID see a list of all possible GO categories that match what you have typed. Then choose a GO category from the list. You can choose multiple domains using CTRL- or CMD-click when choosing the domains.

When using the 'Free Text (use'*' for wildcard)' parameter, type the text term you wish to find and include an asterisk wildcard for ambiguous portions of your text term. (*ase, kin*, *kinase*) The search will query for all terms or IDs whose names, accessions or descriptions contain your text.

transcript.displayName: Orthology Phylogenetic Profile
transcript.description:
Find genes that have a specified orthology-based phylogenetic profile. The phylogenetic profile of a gene is a series of "present" or "absent" calls, reflecting the inclusion of a gene in ortholog groups determined by the OrthoMCL algorithm.

The OrthoMCL algorithm clusters proteins into ortholog groups based on BLAST similarity across at least 150 genomes that span the tree of life. The ortholog groups document protein similarity across many species. Mapping ortholog groups onto the phyletic tree of life provides a framework for correlating protein similarity across species. The other species that are included in that gene's ortholog group can be thought of as a phylogenetic profile.

Use this search to define a pattern across those ortholog groups, and find genes that match that pattern. The pattern is a specification, for each species, of "include", "exclude", or "no constraints." Click on the radio button next to a species to toggle through the three states. A means "include", an means "exclude" and means "no constraints".

For example, to find genes that are present in Apicomplexa but not in humans, click on Apicomplexa until you see a and click on Homo sapiens until you see an .
transcript.summary: Find genes that have an orthology-based phylogenetic profile that you specify.

transcript.displayName: Text (product name, notes, etc.)
transcript.description:
Find genes by searching text annotations. The search compares your term against the text in the fields you specify, returning genes that have a match.

Select the Organism(s) you wish to query and enter your text term. Surround your text term with quotation marks to find exact phrase matches. For example, searching "ABC transporter" will match the exact phrase 'ABC transporter', whereas searching ABC transporter will match ABC and/or transporter. Use an asterisk (*) as a wild card character when looking for plural or compound words. For example, to find all compound words that start with phospho (ie. phosphodiesterase), type phospho* in the search window.

Hints: The search is similar to Google -- if you enter multiple words, genes that match more of those words will have a better score than those that match fewer of the words. If the words are found close together, that also improves the score. Higher scores appear at the top of your result list.

Looking for a list of genes?: If you need to query for a list of gene and you have each gene's ID, use the Identify Genes based on List of IDs search categorized under Genes, Annotation curation and identifiers, List of IDs.

Note about non-relevant results: Depending on how you configure it, this text search may return "non-relevant" genes (false positives). The search mechanically matches the term you supply against the Fields that you choose. The presence of your term in that field does not necessarily mean that the term actually describes the gene. The term may be mentioned in that field for less relevant reasons. To work around this, please carefully choose the Fields you want to search, and then, before drawing any conclusions, review the reference to your term in all matched fields in the gene page to confirm the meaning of its mention. The "Gene product" field is the most stringent and is unlikely to return false positives.
transcript.summary: Find genes with a text search against their product name, notes, GO, EC, Domains, NRDB, or metabolic pathways.

transcript.displayName: Proximity to Telomeres
transcript.description:
Find genes within a given distance from a telomere.

Because telomere sequences are repetitive, they are not included in genome sequences. This search uses the start and end positions of chromosomes as the location of telomeres. When defining parameters for this search, please take into account that the actual location of the telomere is near the end of the chromosome.

First, choose the Organism and Chromosome that you wish to query. Then, enter a Maximum Distance from Telomere. The search will query two genomic regions that are equal in size to your Maximum Distance - one region on each side of the chromosome. The search returns genes found within the two regions.
transcript.summary: Find genes within a given distance from the telomeres (start and end positions) of chromosomes.

transcript.description:

This search returns genes whose protein products have a high BLAST similarity to proteins whose structures have been experimentally determined and deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB).

Then choose the clade of organism whose PDB records should be queried for BLAST similarity. Specify the cutoff for the p-value exponent for the BLAST similarity between the gene and the PDB structure.

transcript.description:
Find genes that have structural predictions at AlphaFold.

AlphaFold predictions are curated by UniProt ID. VEuPathDB uses UniProt IDs to associate AlphaFold predictions with genes. This search returns all genes where at least one of the UniProt IDs associated with the gene appears in the AlphaFold database.

In some cases where specific organisms or genes are not in UniProt, associations between genes and UniProt entries may have been made by sequence similarity. We have endeavoured to indicate where an AlphaFold prediction is associated with a gene through this mechanism.

transcript.displayName: Copy Number (CNV)
transcript.description:
Find genes with a copy number in a resequenced strain that is within a range that you specify.

Whole genome resequencing data was used to estimate each gene's copy number in resequenced strains. This search returns genes that are present at copy numbers (haploid number or gene dose) within a range that you specify.

You have the choice between two different metrics for defining copy number: haploid number or gene dose. Haploid number is the number of genes on an individual chromosome. Gene dose is the total number of genes in an organism, accounting for copy number of the chromosome. For example, a single-copy gene in a diploid organism has a haploid number of 1 and a gene dose of 2. You can choose to search for genes where at least one of your selected isolates meets your cutoff criteria for the chosen metric (By Strain/Sample), or where the median of the chosen metric across all the selected isolates meets the cutoff (Median of Selected Strains/Samples)

Begin by choosing an Organism (reference genome) and one or more resequenced isolates. Choose whether you want to apply your search criteris to individual samples or to the median of your chosen samples. Then choose your Metric, Operator and Copy Number, and initiate the search by clicking the GET ANSWER button. Genes returned by the search will have a copy number based on your chosen metric within the range that you specified. For example, searching with the haploid number equal to 4 will return genes with 4 copies on a chromosome.
transcript.summary: Find genes based on the number of copies in resequenced strains

transcript.displayName: Copy Number Comparison (CNV)
transcript.description:
Find genes by comparing the gene copy number in one or more resequenced strains to its copy number in the reference genome.

Whole genome resequencing was used to estimate each gene's copy number in resequenced strains. This search compares the estimated copy number of a gene in the resequenced strain with the copy number in the reference annotation. The copy number in the reference annotation is calculated as the number of genes that are both on the same chromosome and in the same ortholog group as the gene of interest. We infer that these genes have arisen as a result of tandem duplication of a common ancestor.

In this search, the metric for copy number is the haploid number, which is the number of copies of a gene on a single chromosome.

Begin by choosing an Organism (reference genome), and one or more resequenced strains, then choose how you want to compare the resequenced strains to the reference. You can search for genes where the estimated copy number in the resequenced strains is greater than or equal to, equal to, or less than or equal to the number of copies in the reference genome. You can choose to search for genes where at least one of your selected strains meets your chosen criteria (By Strain/Sample), or where the median across all your selected strains meets the criteria (Median of Selected Strains/Samples) After making your selections, initiate the search by clicking on the GET ANSWER button.

Be cautious using the less than or equal to operator, because regions which do not sequence well may appear to have reductions in gene copy number.

Find genes by comparing the gene copy number in the resequenced strain to its copy

transcript.displayName: L. donovani BPK282A1 Visceral vs cutaneous isolate transcriptomes RNA-Seq (fold change)
transcript.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment. Differential expression is based on the number of unique reads mapped to each gene. First choose an Experiment since the available samples may change between experiments. If there is only one Experiment shown, this field will be selected for you.

Set the directionality of change in expression that you would like to see in the genes returned by this search. Choose to search for up-regulated, down-regulated, or up- and down-regulated genes.

Use the Fold Change >= parameter to set the cutoff for the change in expression for the genes returned by the search.

Choose the samples that you wish to compare. You may choose one or more samples for the reference and comparison. Fold change is calculated between your chosen reference and comparison samples and no statistical analysis is applied. For up-regulated genes the comparison/reference ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For down-regulated genes the reference/comparison ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference. There is an option to search for both up- and down- regulated genes in one query.

After selecting samples you have the option to perform the fold change calulation with the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further.
transcript.summary: Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment.

transcript.displayName: L. braziliensis MHOM/BR/75/M2904 Life Stages Transcriptomes (AMA, META, PRO) RNA-Seq (fold change)
transcript.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment. Differential expression is based on the number of unique reads mapped to each gene. First choose an Experiment since the available samples may change between experiments. If there is only one Experiment shown, this field will be selected for you.

Set the directionality of change in expression that you would like to see in the genes returned by this search. Choose to search for up-regulated, down-regulated, or up- and down-regulated genes.

Use the Fold Change >= parameter to set the cutoff for the change in expression for the genes returned by the search.

Choose the samples that you wish to compare. You may choose one or more samples for the reference and comparison. Fold change is calculated between your chosen reference and comparison samples and no statistical analysis is applied. For up-regulated genes the comparison/reference ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For down-regulated genes the reference/comparison ratio will be greater than the value you specified in the Fold Change parameter. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference. There is an option to search for both up- and down- regulated genes in one query.

After selecting samples you have the option to perform the fold change calulation with the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results). Time series experiments will offer an extra parameter called "Global min/max" which allows you to filter your results further.
transcript.summary: Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment.

transcript.displayName: T. brucei brucei TREU927 Procyclic and bloodstream form mRNA transcriptome and ribosome profiling RNA-Seq (Differential Expression)
transcript.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in an mRNA-Seq experiment as determined by DESeq analysis. Differential expression is based on the number of unique reads for each gene. Please choose experiment. If only one "Experiment" is shown, this field will be selected for you.

Please choose a reference and a comparator sample. You can choose the directionality and the magnitude of the difference by setting both fold change and adjusted p values. For example, selecting up-regulated with a fold difference of 2 and a adjusted p value cut off of 0.1 will only show results where the comparator is twice that of the reference with a adjusted p value of 0.1 or less.

Please note only those samples from your choosen experiment that have at least 2 replicates are shown.
transcript.summary: Find genes which are determined to be differentially expressed by DESeq analysis in an RNA-Seq experiment.

transcript.displayName: T. brucei brucei TREU927 T. brucei procyclic cell cycle proteome Proteomics (fold change)
transcript.description:
Find genes which are differentially expressed in a Proteomics experiment. First choose an experiment as the available samples may change. If only one "Experiment" is shown, this field will be selected for you.

After selecting samples you have the option to take the average, minimum, or maximum expression value within each group. (If choosing only one sample from a group, the selected 'operation' will not affect your results).
